idiom_name: class DialogMediator with MutableMap<String, MutableList<(Any?) -> Unit>>
implementation_notes: Kotlin's mediator is an ordinary class holding the collaborators or a MutableMap of event name to handler list: function types replace the Colleague hierarchy, constructor injection passes the hub to participants, and a single notify entry point keeps the protocol explicit. Classes and members are final by default, so colleagues expose an interface (or a fun interface) rather than a base class, and lambdas mean no subclass explosion. Use this form for local, synchronous coordination; when events must be observed from several coroutines with buffering, replay or back-pressure, the SharedFlow variant is the better fit because a hand-rolled listener list offers no delivery guarantees.
pitfalls: Handlers are strong references: a component that registers on the hub and is never removed stays reachable, so expose remove and deregister in the component's lifecycle (Android: onDestroy).
Iterating the live list while a handler registers or removes throws ConcurrentModificationException; dispatch over a snapshot as above.
Payloads typed Any? push casts into handlers; a sealed interface of event types keeps the protocol compile-time checked.
The hub is not thread-safe (plain MutableMap); if colleagues run on different dispatchers, confine it to one thread or use a concurrent structure.

variants.name: Coroutine SharedFlow event hub
variants.implementation_notes: A shared flow is the mediator's notification channel in coroutine code: the hub owns a MutableSharedFlow (or StateFlow when only the latest state matters), colleagues publish with tryEmit/emit and subscribe by collecting the flow in their own scope; the flow handles fan-out to any number of collectors plus buffering and back-pressure, which a callback list has to fake. Use it when participants live in different coroutines or dispatchers and delivery semantics (replay, extraBufferCapacity, onBufferOverflow) matter; prefer the plain handler map when everything is single-threaded and synchronous, because a Flow brings coroutine scopes, cancellation and collection lifecycle with it.
pitfalls: tryEmit drops the event when the buffer is full and no collector keeps up (check its Boolean result); emit suspends instead, so choose deliberately and size extraBufferCapacity.
A plain MutableSharedFlow has no replay, so a collector that starts after an event never sees it; use replay or StateFlow for state-like signals.
Collecting in a scope that is never cancelled (GlobalScope, an unbound scope) leaks collectors and keeps colleagues alive; tie collection to the component's scope.
SharedFlow is hot and one-way: a mediator that needs a reply needs a second channel or a request flow carrying a replyTo id.
